topic: llmxray: local LLM observability you can install tonight
title: Local LLM Observability: llmxray Reads the Gauges Ollama Publishes
description: Local LLM observability for the Ollama model already running on your PC. One free command, npx llmxray, opens a localhost dashboard that colors every token by generation speed, badges quiet failures, and measures what your prompt layout costs your KV cache. You'll learn how one timestamp at the top of a prompt can drop cache reuse from 290 tokens to 4, why the maintainer's 3.5x faster prefill is an illustration rather than a benchmark, and how Cache Lab runs the same measurement against your own daemon tonight. (Narration is AI-generated.)
hook_candidates: You run Ollama every day. You've never seen one number about it.
Your Ollama model isn't slow. Your prompt layout is.
Three and a half times faster. Same words, one timestamp moved.
One command turns your local model's hidden numbers into gauges.
Free, no cloud, no keys: an instrument panel for your local model.
That timestamp at the top of your prompt is costing you every turn.
Four tokens reused, or two hundred ninety. Same prompt.
Your chat window throws away the most interesting number in the room.
Ollama already publishes gauges on localhost. You've never opened them.
Watch your model think, token by token, tonight.
narration_full: Ollama already publishes gauges on localhost. You've never opened them. You chat with your local model and see only finished words. Underneath, your model writes one token at a time. A token is a small chunk of text it reads and writes piece by piece. How fast each chunk arrives is information. A plain chat window throws all of it away. Now those gauges get a face. A free tool called llmxray, just posted to Hacker News, works like a dashboard for that engine. It needs Ollama running, plus Node.js eighteen or newer. One command, npx llmxray, then a page at localhost, port fifty-one seventy-four. Each token arrives colored by how fast it showed up. That color is a timing approximation, not real probability, and the app says so. A dashboard only displays what sensors report. Badges appear only when something is wrong: repetition, refusal, gibberish, a truncated reply. Now for the cost you never saw. Your chat app resends the same prompt every turn. The maintainer's test prompt was three hundred twenty-four tokens, with a live timestamp near the top. That timestamp changes every turn. That small change is expensive. Now the state flips. The model keeps a saved memory of having read your prompt, the KV cache. It can reuse that memory only while the prompt still matches. Cache Lab, the tool's measurement mode, counted what survived the moving timestamp: four tokens reused. Why so brutal? The cache holds only while the prompt matches from its very first token. One changed value near the top makes a stranger of everything below it. So each turn, the model re-reads nearly the whole prompt before writing. That reading work is called prefill. Now move the timestamp to the back of the same prompt. The words are identical, the order barely changed. But the top of the prompt finally matches turn after turn, so the cache holds. Cache Lab counted two hundred ninety tokens reused. The same words ran three point five times faster, just by moving one timestamp. That's the maintainer's own illustration on one prompt, not a benchmark. But Cache Lab runs against your own daemon, so you can measure your own prompts tonight.

analogy.vehicle: a car dashboard reading an engine's existing sensors
analogy.mapping: Ollama is the engine, already emitting readings on localhost; llmxray is the dashboard that turns those existing readings into colored tokens, gauges, and warning badges
analogy.limit: a dashboard can only display what its sensors report; it cannot fix the engine, and the token color is inferred from timing, not read from a real probability sensor

notes_for_review: Check the voice read of "port fifty-one seventy-four" against the on-screen localhost:5174 so the spoken number and the shown URL agree. Confirm that speaking Node.js "eighteen" is acceptable next to the three assigned key numbers; it is a guardrail-mandated prerequisite, not a metric, but a strict number counter may flag it. Verify the 3.5x hedge lands exactly once and that no banned figures (64.6, 18.6, 4375, 115, 8.9 million) appear in narration or on-screen text.
